title: Distinguish process-wide access from a container registration lifetime and account for concurrency, disposal, and hidden global dependencies

questions.prompt:
In an ASP.NET Core app, `Cache` is registered with `services.AddSingleton<ICache, Cache>()`. During registration, a startup helper calls `services.BuildServiceProvider()` and resolves `ICache` from it to read some settings. The app then builds its normal service provider and serves requests that also resolve `ICache`. Logs show that the `Cache` constructor ran twice.

Explain why the singleton registration did not prevent a second instance.

rubric.point: States that singleton lifetime means one instance per root service provider (container) and registration, not one instance per process.
Explains that calling `BuildServiceProvider` created a second root provider with its own singleton cache, so each provider created its own `Cache` instance.

questions.model: `AddSingleton` is a container lifetime rule: one instance per root provider and registration, not a process-wide guarantee. Calling `BuildServiceProvider` during registration made a second root container with its own singleton set, so it created one `Cache` and the app's real provider created another.

questions.prompt:
A classical Singleton `RequestStats` replaced its hand-written double-checked locking with `private static readonly Lazy<RequestStats> _instance = new(() => new RequestStats());` (default `Lazy<T>` settings). The instance holds a plain `Dictionary<string, int>` that request threads increment concurrently through `RequestStats.Instance`.

Which statement correctly explains the concurrency risk that remains?
options: `Lazy<T>` gives each thread its own instance, so every thread keeps a separate dictionary and the totals diverge.
`Lazy<T>` serializes every member call on the instance, so the only remaining cost is lock contention under heavy load.
`Lazy<T>` makes creation thread-safe so only one instance exists, but unsynchronized writes to its shared dictionary still race.
`Lazy<T>` only delays creation, so two threads arriving together can still each construct an instance and overwrite the field.

rubric.point: Selects the option stating that `Lazy<T>` makes initialization thread-safe (one instance) but does not make the instance's shared mutable state thread-safe.

questions.model:
**C.** Default `Lazy<T>` guarantees one thread-safe construction, removing the double-checked-locking problem. It does nothing for the instance's members: concurrent unsynchronized writes to the shared `Dictionary` still race, so the state needs its own synchronization.

*Optional detail:* swapping `Dictionary` for `ConcurrentDictionary` alone does not make `stats[key]++` atomic, because the read and the write are separate operations. Valid fixes are a `lock` around the whole increment or `ConcurrentDictionary.AddOrUpdate(key, 1, (_, n) => n + 1)`.

c1.feedback: You said you didn't know. The model answer shows what was needed.

c2.feedback: The answer is “`Lazy<T>` makes creation thread-safe so only one instance exists, but unsynchronized writes to its shared dictionary still race.”.
